findings.section: Exam English core words (paragraph 3 and trap how-the-exam-asks-trap-detect-meets-ensure); also 2-deep.md Strength of requirement table row 'ensure' and exam-english.md
findings.quote: The word **ensure** asks for a control that enforces or prevents, not one that only detects. ... **Truth:** "Ensure" asks for a control that prevents the action, even for the root user.
findings.evidence: No fact link, and the exam guide's own use of 'ensure' refutes the rule. Verified fact exam-guide-backup-retention-wording quotes Content Domain 2: 'Implementing strategies to ensure the durability and availability of data (for example, backups)'. A backup does not prevent anything. The same page (docs/aws-certification/latest/solutions-architect-associate-03/solutions-architect-associate-03-domain2) also says 'Determining automation strategies to ensure infrastructure integrity'. So 'ensure' does not by itself mean a preventive control, and 'even for the root user' is not implied by the word at all; it comes from one question's stem (q011, 'including the root user'). A reader who applies the taught rule will reject correct backup, replication or detect-and-remediate answers. Fix: teach that 'ensure' makes the requirement hard; prevention is signalled by words such as 'prevent', 'cannot', 'no one ... can'; keep the root-user point attached to the q011 stem wording, not to the word 'ensure'.
findings.resolution: fix-01: the rule now says that ensure makes a requirement hard and that what follows decides: 'ensure that no one can delete' asks for prevention, 'ensure the durability of data' can be met by backups. Changed: 1-fast core-words paragraph; trap detect-meets-ensure (prevention tied to the stem's 'no one can' wording and to the root user when the stem names it); the ensure row in data/exam-english.json; Check 2 (now tests the backup case, linked to exam-guide-backup-retention-wording); q011 why a, explanation, takeaway and say (explanation-only edits, key unchanged).

findings.section: Optimisation qualifiers (paragraph 2); Confusable words trap how-the-exam-asks-trap-ha-equals-ft; also 1-fast.md Exam English core words paragraph 4 and the qualifiers table rows 'highly available' and 'fault tolerant'
findings.quote: **High availability** (hy uh-vayl-uh-BIL-ih-tee) accepts a short interruption, so automatic failover to a second copy is enough. **Fault tolerance** (FAWLT TOL-er-uns) accepts none, so spare capacity is already running and takes the load without a pause. ... **Truth:** The guide writes [a highly available and/or fault-tolerant architecture across AWS Regions or Availability Zones](../facts/exam.md#exam-guide-highly-available-fault-tolerant-wording): two requirements. Fault tolerant accepts no interruption.
findings.evidence: The linked fact only quotes the guide's phrase 'highly available and/or fault-tolerant'; it does not define either term or say they differ by interruption (the link text is right, the sentence says more). No AWS page in the corpus defines HA as 'a short interruption is acceptable' (search 'fault tolerance (is|refers|means)|high availability (is|refers|means)': no definition). AWS instead uses both words together for automatic failover without interruption: docs/vpc/latest/userguide/disaster-recovery-resiliency 'With Availability Zones, you can design and operate applications and databases that automatically fail over between zones without interruption. Availability Zones are more highly available, fault tolerant, and scalable than traditional single or multiple data center infrastructures.' The 'Truth' is therefore prep-course folklore stated as AWS fact in a trap. Fix: present it as this book's working rule ('In this book ...', no-fact marker), or remove the 'Truth' framing; keep 'read which interruption the stem accepts' as the method.
findings.resolution: fix-01: framed as this book's reading rule in 1-fast ('This book reads them as two strengths ... The stem decides') and in 2-deep (the guide quote now only shows that the guide names both together); the trap Truth no longer says 'two requirements' as AWS fact; the highly available and fault tolerant rows in data/exam-english.json say 'this book'.

findings.section: Optimisation qualifiers (paragraph 1)
findings.quote: So the qualifier also tells you which domain the question tests. MOST secure matters most, because the secure domain is the largest, with [30% of scored content](../facts/exam.md#exam-domain-weights).
findings.evidence: Contradicted by this chapter's own data (data/01-how-the-exam-asks/questions.json): q003, q007, q010, q011 are domain 1 (Secure) with qualifier 'LEAST operational overhead'; q012 is domain 2 (Resilient) with 'MOST cost-effective'; q005 is domain 4 with 'LEAST operational overhead'. The exam guide assigns domains by task statement, not by qualifier word (docs/aws-certification/latest/solutions-architect-associate-03/solutions-architect-associate-03-domain2 lists tasks 'Task 2.1: Design scalable and loosely coupled architectures', 'Task 2.2: Design highly available and/or fault-tolerant architectures'). The 30% fact supports the domain weight, not the conclusion that the MOST secure qualifier 'matters most'. Fix: delete the domain inference; say only that the four qualifier words echo the four domain names.
findings.resolution: fix-01: deleted the domain inference and 'MOST secure matters most'. The paragraph now names the three qualifiers that echo the domain names and says the qualifier does not tell the domain (a security question often asks for LEAST operational overhead).

findings.section: What the exam measures (table row 'Results')
findings.quote: | Results | [within five business days](../facts/exam.md#exam-results-timing); [no pass or fail on screen](../facts/exam.md#exam-no-result-on-screen) |
findings.evidence: exam-no-result-on-screen quote (www/certification/faqs): 'Most AWS Certification exams do not display your pass/fail result at the end of the test.' The display drops 'Most' and turns a hedge into an absolute. It is also a paraphrase, not a verbatim phrase from the quote, which the 2026-10-11 ruling on number-free displays forbids ('copied verbatim from one of the fact's quotes, never a paraphrase'). Fix: use the verbatim display 'do not display your pass/fail result at the end of the test' with 'Most exams' in the sentence, and drop the 'no pass or fail on screen' display from the fact's write-it-as list.
findings.resolution: fix-01: the Results row is split; a new 'On screen' row reads 'most exams [do not display your pass/fail result at the end of the test]' (verbatim display). The fact's short display 'no pass or fail on screen' is left in the fact: removing it is a fact amend (new rev and entail vote) and 00-start-here/calendar.md also links the fact; logged for the registrar.

findings.section: Data and time (paragraph 2 and table rows 'real-time', 'near real-time'; same rows in exam-english.md)
findings.quote: Real-time allows no noticeable delay, so it points to streaming. Near real-time accepts a short delay, so a buffered delivery service is enough.
findings.evidence: AWS describes the buffered delivery service itself as real-time: docs/whitepapers/latest/building-data-lakes/data-ingestion-methods 'Firehose is a fully managed service for delivering real-time streaming data directly to data lakes (Amazon S3), data stores, and analytical services for further processing.' A search of the Firehose developer guide for 'near real-time' returns 0 hits. So the twin is a stem-reading convention, not AWS terminology, and 'real-time ... streaming, not batch' does not separate the two services (both stream). Fix: mark it as this book's reading rule for stems and avoid implying that AWS reserves 'real-time' for one service.
findings.resolution: fix-01: 2-deep now says the twin is a reading rule of this book, not AWS terminology, and to read the delay the stem accepts; rows changed to 'the smallest delay; a reading rule of this book, compare with near real-time' and 'a short delay is allowed, so a service that buffers data can fit'.

findings.section: Data and time table, row 'transactional' (same row in exam-english.md)
findings.quote: | transactional | several changes succeed together or fail together | a relational database, unless the stem also asks for another model |
findings.evidence: docs/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/Introduction: 'You can use DynamoDB transactions to achieve atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability (ACID) across one or more tables with a single request. (ACID) transactions suit workloads that include processing financial transactions or fulfilling orders.' 'Transactional' alone does not point to a relational database; a key-value stem with transactions points to DynamoDB transactions. Fix: 'a database that supports ACID transactions (relational, or DynamoDB transactions)'.
findings.resolution: fix-01: row signal is now 'a database with ACID transactions: a relational engine, or Amazon DynamoDB transactions'.

findings.section: Data and time table, row 'infrequently accessed' (same row in exam-english.md)
findings.quote: | infrequently accessed | people read the data only sometimes | a cheaper storage class with a retrieval charge; check how fast a read must be |
findings.evidence: www/s3/faqs (What is S3 Intelligent-Tiering?): 'There are no retrieval charges in S3 Intelligent-Tiering, so you won’t see unexpected increases in storage bills when access patterns change.' Its Infrequent Access tier is an infrequent-access option without a retrieval charge, and it is the usual answer when the access pattern is unknown. The row teaches 'infrequent = retrieval charge' as a rule. Fix: 'a cheaper storage class; most have a retrieval charge, S3 Intelligent-Tiering has none; check how fast a read must be'.
findings.resolution: fix-01: the rule 'infrequent = retrieval charge' is removed; the signal is now 'a cheaper storage class; check the retrieval charge and how fast a read must be'. No Intelligent-Tiering claim was added: no verified S3 fact exists yet.

findings.section: Confusable words
findings.quote: - **Terminate** (TER-mih-nayt) or stop: terminate deletes the instance; stop pauses it.
findings.evidence: www/ec2/faqs (Hibernate): 'In the case of hibernate, your instance gets hibernated and the RAM data persisted. In the case of Stop, your instance gets shut down and RAM is cleared.' and 'Local instance storage is not persisted.' 'Pauses' describes hibernate, not stop; the exam tests stop vs hibernate (in-memory state). Fix: 'stop shuts it down: the EBS volumes stay, memory and instance store data are lost; hibernate keeps memory'.
findings.resolution: fix-01: now 'terminate deletes the instance; stop shuts it down, which is not a pause.' The EBS and memory detail is not added: the EC2 state and hibernate facts (ec2-state-*, ec2-hibernate-*) are mech-pass, not verified, so they cannot be linked yet.

findings.section: Words customers say
findings.quote: - **cold start**: the delay of the first request, when a function environment starts; "latency", "initialization".
findings.evidence: docs/lambda/latest/dg/lambda-concurrency: 'When Lambda has to initialize a new environment to carry out an invocation, this is known as a cold start.' A cold start happens for any invocation that needs a new environment (for example when the function scales out), not only the first request. Fix: 'the delay when Lambda must start a new execution environment for a request'.
findings.resolution: fix-01: now 'the delay when a function needs a new execution environment for a request'.

findings.section: Read the stem in this order (paragraph 1)
findings.quote: A stem has four parts: context, a problem or change, zero to three constraints, and the ask.
findings.evidence: Stated as a fact about SAA-C03 stems with no fact link; no AWS page in the corpus describes stem anatomy or a constraint count (the exam guide only gives question types and the instruction 'Select one or more responses that best complete the statement or answer the question'). The count 'zero to three' is a number in a method section without a link. Fix: frame as this book's model ('In this book, a stem has ...') or add the no-fact marker per CONVENTIONS-2 decision 33.
findings.resolution: fix-01: now 'In this book, a stem has four parts: context, a problem or change, the constraints, and the ask.' The count is gone.

findings.section: Question 8 (how-the-exam-asks-q007), Why not, option e
findings.quote: It works, but one shared role serves every instance, because a role change [propagates to all of them](../facts/iam.md#iam-ec2-role-credentials-rotate-automatically); extra roles add work.
findings.evidence: iam-ec2-role-credentials-rotate-automatically quote (docs/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_use_switch-role-ec2): 'if you use a single role for multiple instances, you can make a change to that one role and the change propagates automatically to all the instances.' The display 'propagates to all of them' is not in the quote (2026-10-11 ruling: number-free displays are verbatim, never paraphrased; the W14 audit matches word for word). The causal 'because' also says more than the fact: the fact gives a benefit of one shared role, not the reason one role 'serves every instance'. Fix: display 'the change propagates automatically to all the instances' and reword to 'one shared role is less work: a change to it propagates ...'.
findings.resolution: fix-01, partly done: the causal 'because' is gone ('one shared role serves every instance, and a change to that role [propagates to all of them]; separate roles multiply the work'). Still open: the link text is the fact's registered display 'propagates to all of them' (iam-ec2-role-credentials-rotate-automatically, home chapter 03), the only display the lint accepts here. Replacing it with the verbatim 'the change propagates automatically to all the instances' is a fact amend (new rev, new entail vote) for the chapter 03 registrar.

findings.section: Questions 1, 2, 4, 7 and 9: Why not handles
findings.quote: - "Create one NAT gateway in a public subnet ...": It works, but the stem accepts an interruption, and three gateways cost more than one because the number of gateways is billed.
findings.evidence: Rule: an explanation must point at the option it explains. The generated handle truncates options to a prefix that two options share. In Question 4 the handle 'Create one NAT gateway in a public subnet ...' explains the wrong option (one gateway in EACH zone) but reads as the correct answer (one gateway in ONE zone), so the reader sees the answer being rejected. Question 7 uses the same handle for the other option. Questions 1 and 2 show 'Create an interface VPC endpoint for Amazon S3 ...' for two different options, and Question 9 shows 'Add an inbound deny rule for the address ...' twice. Fix in the generator (sync): extend the handle until it is unique among the options, or label options A to D.
findings.resolution: fix-01: each wrong option whose 8-word handle collides now starts its why by naming itself: q002 b 'One gateway in each zone works', q006 a 'One gateway in one zone is the cheapest', q004 b 'One endpoint per zone', q004 c and q008 c 'The endpoint plus a second NAT gateway works', q010 b 'A deny rule in the security group cannot exist', q010 c 'A deny rule in every subnet's network ACL works', q011 c 'Attaching the SCP account by account works'. Explanation-only edits: stems, option texts and keys are unchanged, so the verification stands; q lint 01 is clean. The generator is unchanged because TOOLS-items.md 6.2 fixes the handle as the first 8 words; a unique-prefix handle or option letters are a contract change for the orchestrator.

findings.resolution: fix-01: q005 why c and twin now link vpc-gateway-endpoint-s3-dynamodb-no-privatelink with its display; the q001 and q012 twins now link global-infrastructure-region-isolated-for-fault-tolerance ('designed to be isolated from the other Regions'), added to their facts lists.

findings.section: Exam English core words (paragraph 1); 2-deep.md Instruction grammar table row 'MOST or LEAST in capitals'
findings.quote: **MOST or LEAST in capitals** tells you that more than one option works.
findings.evidence: No fact link and no AWS source: the exam guide only says to 'Select one or more responses that best complete the statement or answer the question' (exam-select-best-response-instruction). A qualifier stem may still have only one option that meets every requirement. Soften to 'often more than one option works; the capital word ranks them'.
findings.resolution: fix-01: 1-fast now says 'usually means that more than one option works'; the exam-English row meaning is 'often more than one option works; rank the options that work'.

findings.section: What the exam measures, trap how-the-exam-asks-trap-esl-after-booking
findings.quote: - **Wrong belief:** You can ask for ESL +30 after you book the exam. **Truth:** You request [ESL +30](../facts/exam.md#exam-esl-accommodation) one time, before you register for an exam.
findings.evidence: Source (www/certification/policies/before-testing): ESL +30 'only needs to be requested once, prior to registering for an exam. It will apply to all future exam registrations with all test delivery providers.' You can ask for it after a booking; it then applies to future registrations, not to the one already booked. The wrong belief as written is literally possible. Better: 'Wrong belief: ESL +30 added later covers an exam you already booked.' The reader has not booked yet, so add what to do if she has (no AWS fact on moving a booking is in the canon; do not invent one).
findings.resolution: fix-01: Wrong belief is now 'ESL +30 requested after booking covers the exam that you booked.'; Truth: ESL +30 is requested before you register, and then it will [apply to all future exam registrations]. Nothing is said about moving a booking (no fact in the canon).

findings.section: Security table, row 'in transit' (same row in exam-english.md)
findings.quote: | in transit | while the data moves over a network | TLS and certificates; a policy can refuse requests that are not encrypted |
findings.evidence: A 'can' claim without a fact. It is true: docs/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/security-best-practices 'We recommend allowing only encrypted connections over HTTPS (TLS) by using the aws:SecureTransport condition in your Amazon S3 bucket policies.' (link markup around aws:SecureTransport removed) Either register a fact (S3 or IAM namespace) and link it from the chapter that teaches it, or keep the vocabulary row free of capability claims.
findings.resolution: fix-01: the capability claim is removed; the signal is now 'TLS and certificates; check whether requests that are not encrypted must be refused'.

findings.section: Question 8 (how-the-exam-asks-q007), Why not option c
findings.quote: AdministratorAccess allows every action on every resource, which breaks least privilege for an application that reads one bucket.
findings.evidence: Absolute claim ('every action on every resource') about an AWS managed policy with no fact link (STYLE strict-text rule for question explanations). The least-privilege half is supported by iam-best-practice-least-privilege-definition ('grant only the permissions required to perform a task'). Link that fact, or register the AdministratorAccess policy content from the IAM managed-policy reference.
findings.resolution: fix-01: q007 why c is now 'AdministratorAccess gives far more than reading one bucket, and least privilege means [defining the actions that can be taken on specific resources under specific conditions](iam-best-practice-least-privilege-definition).' The absolute 'every action on every resource' is gone.
